# Conclusion

This study investigated whether a plant's bioelectric voltage signal can
detect a nearby human's emotional state. A multimodal pilot study with
15 participants was conducted, combining heart rate variability, facial
expression recognition, and ambient CO~2~ as proxy indicators of arousal
and valence. The plant signal was evaluated against these indicators
since no self-reported ground truth was collected.

Across three prediction targets, the plant signal showed a consistent
but modest predictive relationship with human emotion. Valence
classification produced the clearest result (f1 macro = 0.423,
permutation p = 0.005), recognizing all three classes with comparable
reliability. Feature importance was dominated by shape: amplitude-based
descriptors were more important than the absolute voltage level,
suggesting that the model captures genuine signal dynamics rather than
session-specific baseline drift. The five-class emotion label was
likewise statistically significant (p = 0.015), but it was much weaker
in practice due to severe class imbalance toward the dominant neutral
category. Arousal prediction, resting solely on HRV, did not reach
conventional significance (p = 0.055). Session normalization of the
plant features improved performance in most model-target combinations.
This supports the hypothesis that between-session electrode and
baseline drift, rather than emotion-relevant signals, accounted for part
of the raw feature results.

A follow-up analysis addressed the most plausible alternative
explanation for the valence result: that ambient CO~2~, rather than the
plant, tracked the participant's breathing and, thus, their arousal
state. A triangle screening test and a partial Spearman correlation
confirmed that CO~2~ correlates with the plant signal, largely as a
between-session, room-level effect, and with valence independently.
However, the plant-valence association survives controlling for CO~2~
almost unchanged at both the raw and within-session levels. These
results rule out CO~2~ as the driver of the observed effect and
strengthen the case for a genuine plant-human relationship.

These findings must be read against several structural limitations. The
absence of a ground truth means that all results are validated only
against proxy labels. Additionally, the small, single-cohort sample
limits generalizability, to name just two examples. Future work should
prioritize collecting a larger cohort with self-assessment ratings and
directly recording respiration to strengthen the arousal axis. The
design presented in this study should be replicated across a broader
population to determine whether the weak but statistically robust
valence signal detected here reflects a reproducible phenomenon.
